newsitem.title: USA: Mass. unemployment rate cut goes to House floor.
newsitem.headline: Mass. unemployment rate cut goes to House floor.

text.p: Massachusetts House of Representatives is expected to take up a measure this week that would lower the rate employers are charged to pay for unemployment benefits.

The House Commerce and Labor Committee Monday, after a lengthy hearing during which business and labor interests were at odds over whether there is too much or too little money in the Unemployment Insurance (UI) Trust Fund, shipped the measure to the floor, State House News Service reported.

Business leaders argued the Massachusetts economy is healthy enough to lower the payroll tax and still grow the trust fund beyond its current $840 million balance. A cut would send a positive message to companies thinking about locating or expanding in the Commonwealth, they said.
Labor representatives and other opponents argued that the fund should be allowed to reach at least $1.5 billion, enough to cover benefits for an 18-month period, before rates are lowered.

Before the committee was Gov. William Weld's call to trim by $35 the per-worker tax companies pay into the UI trust fund. Lt. Gov. Paul Cellucci testified that the reduction would Massaschusetts more business friendly, saving companies $90 million collectively. With a per-worker tax of $471, Massachusetts has the second highest payroll tax in the country, more than twice the national average.

A rate hike went into effect in January because the Legislature failed to act on another bill that would have frozen UI rates at last year's level. Bill reflecting the hike are due to go out in March.
But the measure may run into trouble in the state Senate.

Senate President Thomas Birmingham, a Democrat, told the committee there will be a downturn economuically and reminded the panel that a $1 billion-plus UI surplus in the late 1980s had quickly evaporated into a $500 million deficit.

"Why drop rates for no good reason?" he asked. Birmingham then noted a $35 savings per worker would mean a business with 10 employees would save $350 a year, and one with 100 workers would have $3,500 in savings.
"Do you really believe those numbers will influence job creation?" he asked.
